1	Representation engineering reveals that sycophancy is linearly encoded in LLM residual streams, suggesting that such directions could serve as training signals for alignment. We test this premise systematically and document its failure. A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$ reliably discriminates sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations, yet every formulation that converts it into a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reward collapses. We identify the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a periodically retrained linear probe on $\dsyc$ is used as a non-differentiable reward signal, behavioral death occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70), creating a 1{,}300-step monitoring blind spot that entropy-based safeguards miss entirely. The failure persists with stopped gradients, implicating the direction's semantic limitation rather than optimization dynamics: $\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}. The failure extends beyond probe rewards: behavioral-reward-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/31 checkpoints, while dense per-token supervised fine-tuning succeeds at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds). A Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ablation identifies supervision granularity as one plausible explanation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_teaser.pdf}
\caption{The probe reward trap. (a)~$\dsyc$ discriminates sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations (AUROC $0.83$), but valid revision and unwarranted capitulation overlap along the same direction. (b)~When used as a GRPO reward, behavioral death (true-positive flip rate $\tof{=}0$) occurs at step 500 while entropy remains healthy; the 1{,}300-step lag renders standard monitoring blind.}
\label{fig:teaser}
\end{figure*}

Sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to prioritize agreement over accuracy, is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy, perez2023discovering}.
Models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) systematically amplify this tendency \citep{ouyang2022instructgpt, christiano2017rlhf, shapira2026amplifies}: even when models can assess the correctness of their own outputs \citep{kadavath2022language}, social pressure from users overrides this internal knowledge \citep{wang2025internal}.
Existing mitigations, from synthetic data augmentation \citep{wei2024synthetic} to neuron-level correction \citep{obrien2025fewbadneurons}, operate on behavioral outputs rather than the internal representations that generate sycophantic decisions.
Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe, marks2024geometry} offers a structurally different approach: a contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of $0.83$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.78$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
If the model's own representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a training signal that targets the computational root of the problem.

We test this hypothesis directly, and find that it fails in a way that standard monitoring cannot detect.
This paper documents the \emph{probe reward trap}: when a periodically retrained linear probe on $\dsyc$ is used as a non-differentiable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reward signal, behavioral death (true-positive flip rate, $\tof = 0$) occurs within 500 steps while generation entropy remains healthy (0.70), masking the failure from standard monitoring (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
In our experiments, the 1{,}300-step lag before distributional collapse means entropy-based early stopping, the most common safeguard against reward hacking \citep{casper2023openproblems}, would miss the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout.
The trap arises even when the probe reward constitutes only a fraction of the total reward signal, reflecting a limitation of $\dsyc$ itself: the direction encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}, so any reward conditioned on it alone will either be gamed or reward rigidity.

The failure is not specific to probe rewards.
Under our GRPO configuration (Qwen3-8B, group size$=$2), cosine projection and continuous probe formulations of $\dsyc$ also collapse, and removing $\dsyc$ entirely does not help: behavioral-reward-only GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4 of 31 checkpoints (12.9\%).
By contrast, Activation Consistency Training \citep[ACT;][]{consistency2025bctact}, which provides dense per-token supervision rather than a single scalar per completion, exceeds vanilla at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
A Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ablation identifies supervision granularity as one plausible explanation for this observed reliability gap.

This paper presents a negative result with systematic diagnostic analysis.
Our three principal findings (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}):

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Observed reliability gap between supervision paradigms} (C1): per-token supervised fine-tuning (SFT) exceeds vanilla at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds; 47/47 including reduced-LoRA ablation). Per-completion GRPO exceeds vanilla at only 4/31 checkpoints (12.9\%). Under matched LoRA, per-token SFT achieves $1.7{\times}$ higher $\sycon$ than per-completion GRPO (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\item \textbf{The probe reward trap} (C2): behavioral death ($\tof{=}0$) precedes distributional collapse by 1{,}300 steps, rendering entropy monitoring blind. The trap arises despite the probe being non-differentiable (stopped gradients), implicating $\dsyc$ itself rather than gradient-based exploitation (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Discriminability does not guarantee reward utility} (C3): $\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}. Valid revision and sycophantic capitulation produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$ \citep{wang2025internal, shapira2026amplifies}, violating the geometric separability that representation-guided RL assumes \citep{burns2023ccs, zhang2026latentgrpo}. Reward overoptimization against such directions produces predictable collapse \citep{gao2023scaling, skalse2022hacking} (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Representation Engineering.}
4	Linear directions in LLM residual streams encode behavioral concepts \citep{zou2023repe, marks2024geometry}; inference-time methods such as Inference-Time Intervention \citep[ITI;][]{li2023iti}, Activation Addition \citep[ActAdd;][]{turner2023actadd}, and Contrastive Activation Addition \citep[CAA;][]{rimsky2024caa} demonstrate that activation geometry suffices for behavioral control \citep{burns2023ccs}, but we find that $\dsyc$ fails when used as an RL reward despite succeeding at inference time.
5	
6	\paragraph{Reward Design and Overoptimization.}
7	Proxy rewards diverge from true objectives under sustained optimization \citep{gao2023scaling, pan2022effects}; \citet{manheim2019goodhart} taxonomize four variants of Goodhart's Law.
8	This risk compounds in RLHF pipelines \citep{christiano2017rlhf, stiennon2020summarize, ziegler2019finetuning}, where policy optimization \citep{schulman2017ppo} amplifies misspecification \citep{hubinger2024sleeper}.
9	Our probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) instantiates the regressional variant, with two features not previously documented: behavioral death within 500 steps (far faster than gradual degradation~\citep{gao2023scaling}) and a 1{,}300-step temporal decoupling that renders entropy monitoring ineffective~\citep{skalse2022hacking}.
10	\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} show that representation-level directions succeed when behaviors are geometrically separable (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
11	
12	\paragraph{Sycophancy Characterization and Mitigation.}
13	Sycophancy is pervasive in assistants trained via RLHF \citep{ouyang2022instructgpt, bai2022training, sharma2023sycophancy, perez2023discovering, shapira2026amplifies} and traceable to late-layer preference shifts \citep{wang2025internal}; it undermines broader truthfulness objectives \citep{lin2022truthfulqa} even when models possess the knowledge to respond accurately \citep{kadavath2022language}.
14	Mitigations span synthetic data \citep{wei2024synthetic}, consistency training \citep{consistency2025bctact}, and neuron-level correction \citep{obrien2025fewbadneurons}.
15	\citet{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} show that sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors; a single $\dsyc$ captures only their shared variance, which is why the step from diagnosis to reward is structurally blocked.
16	
17	\paragraph{Probe-Based and Representation-Guided Methods.}
18	\citet{papadatos2024probepenalties} reduce sycophancy via Best-of-N reranking with linear probe penalties (94\% accuracy) without producing gradients; our work reveals what happens when a comparable signal enters the training loop (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
19	Representation-guided RL has been extended to reasoning and gradient regularization \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo, luo2026craft, sinii2025smallvectors, ackermann2026gradreg}.
20	SMART \citep{beigi2025smart} applies per-step process rewards for sycophancy, succeeding where our completion-level rewards fail, consistent with ACT's per-token success and with broader evidence that process supervision outperforms outcome supervision \citep{lightman2024verify, uesato2022solving}.
21

1	\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
4	The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
5	$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
6	The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
7	Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
8	The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
9	These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
10	Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
11	This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
12	\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
13	Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\section{When Does Discriminability Fail as Reward Utility?}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Root cause of the probe reward trap.}
The probe reward trap (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) and the cosine failures (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}) share a common geometric root.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation generalizes: Llama-3-8B achieves comparable discriminability (AUROC $0.779$) yet the semantic gap persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve.
\citet{wu2026rewardhacking} reinforce this principle: concept directions succeed when shortcut behaviors are geometrically separable.
Independent work corroborates the limitation: persona vectors are geometrically independent of $\dsyc$ \citep{kelkar2026persona}, and sycophancy decomposes into independently steerable sub-behaviors \citep{vennemeyer2025sycophancy} that $\dsyc$ projects onto a single axis.

\section{Direction Discriminability}
\label{sec:direction_quality}

Before evaluating $\dsyc$ as a reward signal (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}--\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}), we first establish that it captures a genuine sycophancy-related signal in the residual stream.
If the direction failed to discriminate sycophantic from non-sycophantic activations, downstream reward failures would be trivially explained by poor direction quality rather than by a fundamental gap between discriminability and reward utility.
We evaluate discriminability along five axes: cross-validated classification accuracy, evidence-strength stratification, cross-model transfer, training stability, and probe ablation.
Figure~\ref{fig:direction_quality} summarizes the per-layer AUROC profiles for both models.

\paragraph{Qwen3-8B layer-wise discriminability.}
We evaluate $\dsyc$ via 5-fold cross-validated AUROC on 181 style-controlled contrastive pairs (\S\ref{ssec:extraction}).
The direction achieves AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ (5-fold CV) at its best layer (L19).
Discriminability emerges gradually across depth: layers L0--L8 perform near chance, statistical significance ($p < 0.01$) first appears at L16, and performance peaks at L19.
This gradual emergence, with the peak in the upper third of the network, suggests that sycophancy-relevant information is encoded as a late-stage representation rather than an input-level confound.
AUROC increases monotonically with evidence-strength tier: from 0.675 on weak-evidence pairs to 0.883 on medium and 0.929 on strong pairs.
This monotonic relationship reflects effect-size differences (stronger evidence produces larger behavioral gaps that are easier to classify) rather than indicating that $\dsyc$ encodes evidential warrant per se.

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
To rule out that these results are specific to Qwen3-8B's representation geometry, we repeat the full extraction and evaluation pipeline on Llama-3-8B-Instruct \citep{touvron2023llama, grattafiori2024llama3}.
Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares the two models.
Llama-3-8B achieves AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$ (5-fold CV) at L16, with a parallel evidence-strength gradient (weak 0.711, medium 0.864, strong 0.911).
The best-layer depth differs (L16 vs.\ L19), consistent with the architectural differences between the two families, but the qualitative pattern is identical: gradual emergence, best-layer selection in the upper third, and monotonic strength scaling.
Discriminability is robust across knowledge domains, with per-domain AUROCs on Llama-3-8B ranging from 0.751 (geography) to 0.844 (commonsense).
When surface confounds (response length, hedging patterns) are explicitly controlled, Llama-3-8B's AUROC rises to 0.923, which confirms that the direction captures semantic content rather than stylistic artifacts.
The consistent results across architecturally distinct model families indicate that contrastive sycophancy directions reflect a shared representational phenomenon rather than a model-specific idiosyncrasy.

\paragraph{Training stability and probe ablation.}
Two additional analyses confirm the robustness of $\dsyc$ under training dynamics.
First, we track direction drift during LoRA fine-tuning: at step 500, the cosine similarity between the original and re-extracted $\dsyc$ is approximately 0.96, and per-layer AUROC remains above 0.77.

\section{Cosine \texorpdfstring{$\rone$}{R1}: Structural Failure}
\label{sec:cosine_failure}

During GRPO training, 256-token truncation reduces $\dsyc$ AUROC from 0.827 to approximately 0.60, so the optimizer works with a substantially weaker signal than the offline metrics suggest.
We test whether even this degraded discriminability translates into a viable reward through four configurations that form a diagnostic chain (Table~\ref{tab:cosine_chain}): each resolves the failure mode of its predecessor but exposes a deeper limitation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cosine $\rone$ failure chain on Qwen3-8B (LoRA rank$=$64, GRPO with $R = w_1 \cdot \rone + w_3 \cdot \rthree$).}
\label{tab:cosine_chain}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lllll@{}}
\toprule
Config & $\rone$ Formula & $w_1$ & Outcome & Root Cause \\
\midrule
F1a & $\tanh(\mathbf{h}\cdot\dsyc/20)$ & 0.25 & Gate saturation & Norm mismatch \\
F1b & $\cos(\mathbf{h},\, \dsyc)$ & 0.25 & $\rone \approx 0$ & Gap too small \\
F1c & +recalibration & 0.25 & Mode collapse & Reward discontinuity \\
F1d & $5\cos(\mathbf{h},\, \dsyc)$ & 0.40 & Mode collapse & $\rthree$ saturation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The diagnostic chain begins with a norm mismatch.
F1a's dot-product formulation ($\rone = \tanh(\mathbf{h} \cdot \dsyc / 20)$) saturates because residual-stream norms exceed the direction norm by $100$--$1{,}200{\times}$, zeroing the gradient by step 955.
Cosine similarity (F1b) eliminates this norm dependence but reveals a second problem: the gap between valid and sycophantic cosines averages only 0.098, too narrow for meaningful reward contrast.
Recalibration (F1c, \S\ref{ssec:recalib}) widens the gap (offline AUROC rises to 0.910) but introduces a third: each recalibration event creates a reward discontinuity that destabilizes advantage estimates, collapsing entropy to 0.069 within 300 steps.
Amplification (F1d, $5{\times}$ scaling) lifts $\rone$ above the noise floor but surfaces the fundamental limitation: $\rthree$ saturates at 0.9998 by step 300, leaving the noisy $\rone$, which conflates warranted revision with unwarranted capitulation, as the sole gradient source until terminal collapse at step 2160.

Truncation further degrades the signal: under the 256-token maximum completion length used in GRPO, $\dsyc$ AUROC drops from 0.76 (full response) to 0.60, so the offline discriminability (0.827) substantially overestimates the signal available during training.
Checkpoint-level evaluation confirms immediate collapse: $\tof{=}0$ from step 500 onward with no stable phase.
The probe reward trap (C2, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}) arises within GRPO using full-length responses and is unaffected by this truncation limitation.
The four configurations converge on a single conclusion: $\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not whether that change is \emph{warranted}.
Valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along $\dsyc$, so the cosine projection assigns similar scores to both.
This is not a calibration artifact (recalibration improves discriminability yet rewards still fail) but a semantic limitation of any continuous $\dsyc$-based reward.
Section~\ref{sec:probe_trap} examines whether discretizing the signal via a binary probe can escape this limitation.

1	\section{The Probe Reward Trap}
2	\label{sec:probe_trap}
3	
4	The cosine formulations fail on signal magnitude; a natural response is to discretize.
5	Training a logistic probe on $\dsyc$ and thresholding its output yields $\rone = \mathbb{I}[P(\text{syc} \mid \mathbf{h}) < 0.5]$ (F2 in \S\ref{ssec:reward}).
6	We show that this discretization sidesteps the magnitude problem but creates a qualitatively worse failure.
7	Both probe experiments use the probe as a non-differentiable reward component within GRPO (\S\ref{ssec:reward}); the trap therefore reflects a semantic limitation of the probe rather than gradient-based exploitation.
8	
9	\paragraph{Differentiable probe: gradient gaming.}
10	Without stop-gradient, the policy discovers within ${\sim}30$ steps that shifting activations away from the sycophancy cluster maximizes $\rone$ regardless of response content, producing an inverted profile ($\tof = 0.978$, $\nof = 0.006$).
11	This motivates the stopped-gradient design below.
12	
13	\paragraph{Binary probe: the stubbornness trap.}
14	With stop-gradient, the policy cannot game the boundary but instead exploits a deeper flaw: $\dsyc$ does not condition on input validity, so refusing to revise a wrong answer receives the same $\rone = 1$ as correctly resisting invalid pressure.
15	By step 500, $\tof$ drops to 0.000 and $\nof$ reaches 0.995, yielding $\sycon = 0$.
16	Qualitative analysis of 181 valid-correction responses reveals five failure modes: \emph{deliberation traps} (28.7\%), where the model identifies the correct answer but cannot commit; \emph{sycophantic stubbornness} (24.3\%), where the model verbally agrees but does not change its answer; \emph{acknowledge-but-maintain} (23.8\%); \emph{genuine-accept-missed} (18.8\%); and refute/ignore/other (4.5\%). Full taxonomy in Appendix~\ref{app:taxonomy}.
17	
18	\paragraph{Behavioral death precedes distributional collapse.}
19	
20	\begin{table}[t]
21	\centering
22	\caption{Probe reward trap trajectory (stopped-gradient probe). Behavioral death ($\tof{=}0$) occurs at step 500; entropy remains healthy until step ${\sim}1840$. Reward averages $+0.72$ throughout.}
23	\label{tab:probe_trajectory}
24	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
25	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
26	\toprule
27	Step & $\tof$ & $\nof$ & $\sycon$ & Entropy & Reward \\
28	\midrule
29	500 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 0.000 & 0.702 & +0.72 \\
30	1000 & 0.006 & 0.995 & 0.011 & 0.800 & +0.71 \\
31	1500 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 0.608 & +0.69 \\
32	2000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 0.304 & +0.69 \\
33	\bottomrule
34	\end{tabular}}
35	\end{table}
36	
37	\begin{figure}[t]
38	\centering
39	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_probe_trap.pdf}
40	\caption{Probe reward trap (stopped-gradient probe). $\tof$ drops to zero at step 500 while generation entropy remains high (0.70--0.80 through step 1000). The 1{,}300-step lag means standard entropy monitoring misses the behavioral failure entirely.}
41	\label{fig:probe_trap}
42	\end{figure}
43	
44	Table~\ref{tab:probe_trajectory} and Figure~\ref{fig:probe_trap} reveal a 1{,}300-step lag between behavioral and distributional collapse.
45	At step 500, the model is behaviorally dead ($\tof = 0$) yet entropy remains high (0.70--0.80) through step 1000, well within the range that standard monitors would flag as healthy, and the combined reward averages $+0.72$ because both $\rone$ and $\rthree$ reinforce non-flipping.
46	Entropy does not collapse until step ${\sim}1840$.
47	This gap carries a practical warning: entropy-based early stopping, the most common safeguard against reward hacking~\citep{casper2023openproblems}, would miss the failure entirely.
48	Detecting probe reward traps requires behavioral monitoring (periodic $\tof$ evaluation), not distributional monitoring alone.
49	
50	\paragraph{A dilemma for direction-based rewards.}
51	The differentiable and binary failures bracket the design space.
52	With gradients, the policy games the boundary; without gradients, it exploits the fact that stubbornness and genuine resistance are indistinguishable along $\dsyc$.
53	Any reward conditioned only on $\dsyc$ (continuous or discrete, differentiable or frozen) will either be gamed or will reward rigidity.
54	Escaping this dilemma requires a signal that incorporates the evidential warrant of the user's challenge, a dimension that $\dsyc$ does not encode~\citep{denison2024subterfuge}.

# ARR Reviewer Guidelines: Key Evaluation Framework

## What to Evaluate

Reviewers should assess papers across multiple dimensions:

**Soundness & Technical Quality**: Validate methodology, proof correctness, and experimental rigor. Check for "appropriate information about statistical significance (error bars, confidence intervals)" and proper assumptions.

**Novelty & Contribution**: Evaluate whether the work advances knowledge. The guidelines caution against dismissing contributions simply because they seem "obvious in retrospect" or aren't state-of-the-art.

**Scope & Appropriateness**: Ensure "claims are appropriately scoped" and the research question is clear.

## Scoring System

ARR uses three distinct scores:

1. **Soundness**: Must be "justified by the text of the review." Low scores require documented technical flaws.

2. **Excitement**: Reflects personal interest, separate from soundness. A paper can be sound but personally unexciting.

3. **Overall Recommendation**: "A composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact."

## Characteristics of Strong Reviews

Effective reviews are:
- **Specific**: "The paper is missing references X, Y, Z" rather than vague criticisms
- **Professional**: Maintain "neutral" tone; "write the review you would like to get yourself"
- **Justified**: Connect scores to documented evidence
- **Constructive**: Explain *why* issues matter, not just listing them

## Guidance on Negative Results

The guidelines explicitly encourage negative results papers: "The bias towards publishing only positive results is a known problem in many fields." Reviewers should evaluate whether findings are "systematically" important, regardless of outcome direction.

## Common Review Pitfalls to Avoid

Problematic patterns flagged include:
- Dismissing work as "too simple" (simplicity is preferable)
- Requesting excessive experiments beyond claim scope
- Criticizing methodology preferences rather than soundness
- Conflating acknowledged limitations with fundamental flaws

本文研究将 LLM 残差流中的对比性 sycophancy 方向 (d_syc) 转化为 GRPO 训练奖励信号的可行性，系统性地记录了其失败模式。核心发现"probe reward trap"表明：当 d_syc 作为二值化 probe 奖励时，行为性死亡 (ToF=0) 比分布性崩溃提前 1,300 步发生，使得基于 entropy 的监控手段完全失效。论文还报告了 per-token SFT (ACT) 在每个 checkpoint 都优于 vanilla，而 per-completion GRPO 仅在极少数 checkpoint 优于 vanilla 的观察。论文将失败归因于 d_syc 的语义局限：它编码"belief 是否改变"而非"是否应该改变"。

---

## 2. Strengths

**S1. 系统性的诊断链设计 (Section 5)**
Cosine R1 的四配置诊断链 (F1a→F1b→F1c→F1d) 设计精巧：每个配置解决前一个的失败模式却暴露更深层问题，最终收敛于 d_syc 的语义局限这一统一结论。这种"逐层剥洋葱"的实验设计让读者清晰追踪作者的推理过程，是本文方法论上的亮点。

**S2. Temporal decoupling 发现具有实践价值 (Section 6, Table 3, Figure 3)**
行为死亡先于分布崩溃 1,300 步的发现有明确的实践意义：entropy-based early stopping 是当前 reward hacking 防护的主流手段 (Casper et al., 2023)，本文指出这一手段对特定类型的 reward 失效有系统性盲区。Table 3 清晰展示 ToF 在 step 500 归零而 entropy 在 0.70-0.80 区间维持到 step 1000+，证据充分。

**S3. 负面结果的诚实报告与充分讨论**
论文没有回避失败，对三类贡献 (C1-C3) 的 scope 做了合理限定。Limitations 部分系统性地讨论了 group size、truncation、single seed、ACT vs GRPO confounds 等问题，体现了学术诚信。"one plausible explanation" 的措辞虽然重复（见 W5），但反映了对因果推断的谨慎态度。

**S4. d_syc 方向的充分验证 (Section 4)**
在声称 d_syc 作为奖励失败之前，Section 4 从五个维度验证了其判别能力（交叉验证、evidence-strength 分层、跨模型迁移、训练稳定性、probe ablation），排除了"方向本身质量差"这一平凡解释。这一实验设计逻辑严谨。

**S5. 对 Vennemeyer et al. (2025) 的整合**
论文在 Related Work 和 Discussion 中都引用了 Vennemeyer et al. (2025) 关于 sycophancy 可分解为独立可操控子行为的发现，并将其与 d_syc 投影到单一轴的局限性联系起来（Section 7, line 13）。这一关联有助于解释为什么 d_syc 在判别上有效但在奖励设计上失败。

---

## 3. Weaknesses

### Must-Fix 问题（影响接收决定）

**N1** [critical] 核心数字不一致：4/31 vs 4/28

- 具体位置：Abstract (line 1)、Introduction C1 (line 31)、Conclusion (line 4) 使用 "4/31 checkpoints (12.9%)"；Discussion (line 45) 和 Table 4 脚注使用 "4/28 checkpoints (14.3%)"
- 问题：论文在最核心的实验结果上使用了两个不同的分母（31 vs 28）和百分比（12.9% vs 14.3%），没有任何解释。通过 Table 5 可以推断 4/31 = 4/28 (gs=2) + 0/3 (gs=8)，但这一合并逻辑从未在正文中说明。更严重的是，在 Conclusion 中"d_syc conflates warranted revision... causing all GRPO formulations to collapse (4/31 checkpoints > vanilla)"这句话将 d_syc 的语义局限归因为所有 GRPO 失败的原因，但 R3-only GRPO 根本不使用 d_syc——这是因果归因错误，不仅仅是数字不一致。
- 为什么影响接收：论文的两个关键 claim（R3-only GRPO 失败率、d_syc 导致所有 GRPO 崩溃）在正文不同位置相互矛盾，损害可信度。
- 建议修改方向：(1) 统一使用一个分母并说明包含/排除 gs=8 的理由；(2) 修正 Conclusion 的因果归因，区分 d_syc 导致的失败（cosine/probe GRPO）和 per-completion 结构导致的失败（R3-only GRPO）。

**N2** [critical] 新颖性定位不够锐利——"probe reward trap" vs Goodhart's Law regressional variant

- 具体位置：Section 2 (Related Work, line 9)、Section 7 (Discussion, line 4-9)
- 问题：论文在 Related Work 中明确将 probe reward trap 定位为 Goodhart's Law 的 regressional variant (Manheim & Garrabrant, 2019)，声称的差异化在于：(a) 行为死亡速度快（500 步 vs 渐进退化），(b) temporal decoupling。但论文没有充分论证为什么这些差异不仅仅是 degree 的区别而是 kind 的区别。快速崩溃可能是 group size=2 + 小数据集（181 pairs）+ LoRA rank 64 等超参数组合的结果，而非本质性的新现象。C3 ("discriminability ≠ reward utility") 虽然表述得当，但本质上是 "good classifier ≠ good reward" 的重述——这在 reward misspecification 文献中是已知原理。
- 为什么影响接收：如果核心贡献被认为是已知原理在特定设定下的确认（而非新发现），论文的 excitement 会显著降低。
- 建议修改方向：(1) 更锐利地定位增量贡献：强调 temporal decoupling 的监控意义（这是最有价值的独特发现），而非泛泛的 "discriminability ≠ reward utility"；(2) 讨论快速崩溃是否在不同超参数下复现，以排除这是超参数artifact的可能；(3) 与 Goodhart taxonomy 的其他 variant 做更精确的对比，说明为什么 regressional variant 在 representation-based reward 设定下有特殊的 failure signature。

**N3** [critical] Probe reward trap 仅有单一 seed 证据

- 具体位置：Limitations (line 4)："The probe reward trap (C2) is demonstrated with a single seed; replication would strengthen the temporal decoupling finding."
- 问题：论文的标题和核心贡献 (C2) 基于单一 seed 的实验。1,300-step temporal decoupling 是本文最独特的发现，但单一 seed 无法区分这是系统性现象还是随机波动。尤其是 R3-only GRPO 在 2 seeds 之间已经显示出显著的 oscillation (Δ≈0.069, Figure 4)，说明训练动态在不同 seed 间变化较大。
- 为什么影响接收：以单一 seed 支撑标题级 claim，不满足实证研究的基本 reproducibility 要求。
- 建议修改方向：至少增加 2 个额外 seed 的 probe trap 实验（计算量不大：单 seed probe trap 在 2000 步内完成，论文报告总计算量仅 ~120 GPU-hours）。如果时间不允许，应显著弱化标题和 Abstract 中对 temporal decoupling 精确步数的声明。

### Should-Fix 问题（影响评分但不一票否决）

**W1** [major] ACT vs GRPO 比较的 confounds 削弱 C1

- 具体位置：Discussion (line 86-88)、Limitations (line 7)、Table 6
- 问题：ACT 和 GRPO 在至少 5 个维度上不同：(1) 序列长度 (1024 vs 256 tokens), (2) 数据来源 (curated pairs vs online generations), (3) dropout (0.05 vs 0), (4) LoRA α (128 vs 64) 和模块数 (7 vs 4), (5) 监督粒度 (per-token vs per-completion)。LoRA-controlled ablation (Table 5) 仅控制了第 (4) 点。论文使用 "one plausible explanation" 来 hedge，但 C1 在 Introduction 中的表述 "Observed reliability gap between supervision paradigms" 暗示这是一个关于 paradigm 差异的 claim，实际证据不足以支撑。
- 建议：(1) 将 C1 的表述从 paradigm-level claim 调整为 observation-level claim；(2) 讨论序列长度 confound 的影响（256 tokens 截断使 d_syc AUROC 从 0.76 降到 0.60，ACT 用 1024 tokens 不受此影响）。

**W2** [major] Framing 在三种叙事之间游移

- 问题：论文在以下三种 framing 之间不够一致：
  - (a) 标题 "The Probe Reward Trap" → 聚焦于特定现象的发现
  - (b) Introduction line 27 "This paper presents a negative result with systematic diagnostic analysis" → negative result paper
  - (c) Conclusion 的核心句 "The broader lesson is that discriminability does not guarantee reward utility" → 通用原则的提炼

- 具体位置：Conclusion (line 4)
- 问题：Conclusion 写道 "The failure is semantic: d_syc conflates warranted revision with unwarranted capitulation, causing all GRPO formulations to collapse (4/31 checkpoints > vanilla) while per-token SFT succeeded at every checkpoint (31/31 across two seeds)." 但 R3-only GRPO (不使用 d_syc) 的失败不能归因于 d_syc 的语义局限。论文在 Discussion 中正确地将其归因于 per-completion 奖励结构的不足，但 Conclusion 的因果归因不一致。

- 具体位置：Abstract (line 1)、Introduction (line 25)、Discussion (line 56, 88)

- 建议：第一次使用 "one plausible explanation" 并充分讨论，后续引用回指即可（如 "as discussed in §7"）。

## 4. Questions to Authors

**Q1.** Probe reward trap 的 temporal decoupling (1,300 步) 在不同 random seed 下是否稳定？如果有额外 seed 的数据，能否提供 behavioral death 时间点的方差？

- **Belinkov (2022)** "Probing Classifiers: Promises, Shortcomings, and Advances" — probing 综述，与本文 "discriminability ≠ reward utility" 论点高度相关
